transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Well, um, I guess the main reason I’m here—and it honestly feels a little embarrassing to even say out loud, but it’s really becoming a major issue for me at work. I’m a kindergarten teacher, you see, and as you can probably imagine with that age group, there are always celebrations, birthdays, school events, that sort of thing going on. 

But what brings me in is that... well, the second I spot balloons at school, I have this intense reaction. I mean, even if they're all the way across the hallway, like down by the main office or the cafeteria and nowhere near my actual classroom, my chest just completely tightens up. It's this instant, overwhelming physical thing. I literally just freeze. I stand there for a moment, completely locked up, before I can even begin to think clearly about what I’m actually supposed to be doing—like whether I was getting my kids lined up for recess, or walking to the copy room, or whatever it was. The exact second I see one, it just derails my brain completely and I just freeze up.
Do you have a similar reaction to anything else, or is it just balloons that cause this response?

No, it's really just the balloons. I mean, I've tried to think about this a lot, wondering if maybe there's something else that sets me off like that. Like, you know, loud noises in general, because kindergarten classrooms can get incredibly loud. Sometimes the kids are screaming or banging blocks together, or someone drops a heavy bin of toys, and that startles me, sure, but it's just a normal startle, you know? It's not that same paralyzing, chest-tightening feeling. 

And I thought maybe it was things that pop, like bubble wrap? But no, my kids love popping bubble wrap when we do sensory activities, and that doesn't bother me at all. It's so specific. It’s literally just balloons. Mylar ones, latex ones, big ones, small ones... just the sight of them. It's so strange because I can handle all the chaos of twenty five-year-olds running around, but put one balloon in the corner of the room, and I'm just a wreck. I can't focus on anything else. So, yeah, I've really racked my brain trying to find a connection to something else, but it's exclusively balloons.
Is there a particular event or memory from your past that you associate with balloons?

Yeah, actually, there is. And it wasn't even from when I was a kid or anything, which is why it feels so silly that it's affecting me this much now. It started about... gosh, let me think. It was right before our spring break, so it's been going on for about seven months now. 

We were having this big children's art celebration at the school. It’s this massive event we do every year where we basically turn the entire gymnasium into a giant art gallery. The kids work on these projects for weeks, and the parents come in, and there's just so much going on. To make it look festive, the PTA had set up these enormous balloon arches at all the entrances. Which, you know, usually I wouldn't think twice about. I think I even helped tape some of them to the wall the afternoon before. 

But anyway, during the actual event, the gym was incredibly crowded and loud. I was standing right near the main entrance, talking to one of my student's parents—I think it was Leo's mom, we were discussing this beautiful watercolor he did—and I had backed up a little too close to one of the arches to let some people walk past us. And... well, I don't know if someone bumped into it, or if it was just over-inflated, or maybe one of the older siblings poked it with something, but one of the really big balloons just... burst. 

But it wasn't just a normal pop from across the room. It was right next to my head. I mean, literally inches from my face. The sound was just deafening, and I could actually feel the air and the snap of the rubber right against my cheek. It was so incredibly sudden, and it completely terrified me. I actually dropped the clipboard I was holding, and my heart was just pounding out of my chest. I had to excuse myself and go sit in the staff room for like twenty minutes just to stop shaking. And ever since that exact moment, about seven months ago, I just... I can't even look at a balloon without my body reacting like that all over again.
Do you find yourself avoiding places or events where you think balloons might be present?

Yeah, I really do try to avoid them, which is, you know, incredibly hard when you work in an elementary school. It’s actually getting to the point where I have to plan my whole day around the possibility of them being there. 

Like, lately, we have this whole routine for birthdays in my classroom. The parents almost always want to bring in cupcakes and, of course, a big shiny balloon for the birthday kid. So I've actually had to start pulling my classroom aides aside—Sarah and Jessica, they're just wonderful, thank goodness for them—and I've been asking them to completely take over the birthday circles. I usually just make up an excuse, like I need to prep the next phonics activity or run to the restroom, and I just let them handle the singing and the handing out of the treats while I stay far away. 

And it's not just in my classroom, either. We had this fall festival thing out on the blacktop last week, and they had these tables set up for face painting and ticket sales, and they had tied these giant helium balloons to the corners of the tables so people could find them easily. I saw them bouncing around in the wind from across the yard, and I just... I immediately started moving away from those tables. I was actually supposed to be supervising that specific zone, but I just kept pacing around the complete opposite side of the playground because I couldn't bring myself to go near them. 

But the hardest part is that sometimes I can't just leave or avoid it. Sometimes a kid will walk right up to my desk holding one, or I'll be stuck in the middle of an assembly, and if I absolutely have to stay, I just... I try to put as much physical distance between me and the balloon as I possibly can. I'll take a few huge steps back, and I just completely fixate on something else. I'll stare at my shoes, or the whiteboard, or a spot on the floor, and I just focus all my energy on getting through those next few minutes without actually looking at it. I just keep repeating in my head, "Don't look at it, just get through this," and it takes everything I have just to endure it until it's gone. It's just so exhausting to constantly be on high alert like that, you know?
Do you ever feel anxious or on edge when you're not around balloons?

No, not really. I mean, I've always been a pretty relaxed person, honestly. You kind of have to be when you spend your days with twenty little kids who are constantly finger-painting and spilling juice and having meltdowns because their graham cracker broke in half. You just learn to roll with the punches. So, no, in my day-to-day life, when I'm just at home, or running errands, or hanging out with my husband—oh, his name is Mark, by the way, he's been so supportive through all of this, even though I know he thinks it's a little bizarre—but when I'm just doing normal things and there are no balloons around, I feel completely fine. 

I don't have this lingering sense of dread or anything. I sleep well, I eat well, I enjoy my weekends. It really is just that specific trigger. Like, if I know I'm going somewhere safe, like the grocery store—well, actually, sometimes the floral department has those Mylar ones, so I do tend to walk down a different aisle just in case—but generally speaking, if I'm not in a situation where I think a balloon is going to suddenly appear, I'm totally relaxed. I don't sit around worrying about my health or my finances or anything else like that. It's just... it's just the balloons. That's the only thing that makes me feel like my heart is going to jump out of my chest.
Have you ever avoided a significant event or activity because of the possibility of balloons being present?

Well, yeah, actually... yes. It's... it's definitely starting to get in the way of things, especially at work. Like I was saying about the birthdays, handing those off to Sarah and Jessica—my aides—it's not just a one-time thing anymore. It's every single time a kid has a birthday, which in a class of twenty, happens pretty often. And I feel terrible because, you know, as a kindergarten teacher, you're supposed to be the one leading the singing and making the birthday kid feel special. It's a huge part of building that classroom community, and I'm just... I'm missing it. I have to step out or hide in the back, and I know the kids notice that I'm not the one handing out the cupcakes anymore.

And then there was that fall festival I mentioned earlier. The thing is, I wasn't just supposed to be generally supervising that zone. I had actually spent weeks planning this really elaborate, messy, fun art table for the kids. We were going to do this big collaborative mural with sponge painting, and I had bought all the supplies, mixed all the colors, everything. I was so excited about it. But then I got out there, and I saw those giant helium balloons tied to the ticket tables right next to my art station. They were just whipping around in the wind, and I... I completely panicked. I couldn't go over there. I just couldn't do it. 

So I ended up having to grab one of the parent volunteers at the last second—I think it was Chloe's dad, bless him—and I just kind of shoved the instructions at him and told him I had to go monitor the bounce house line instead. Which was totally on the other side of the blacktop. And it was awful, because I missed out on doing the activity I had planned, and the worst part is... my principal, Mrs. Higgins, she definitely noticed. She actually pulled me aside the next day and asked why I wasn't running the art table like we had discussed at the staff meeting. I just mumbled something about needing extra coverage by the bounce houses, but I know she didn't really buy it. It's just so embarrassing that I'm letting this... this fear... actually affect my job and how my supervisor sees me, you know? It's just getting to be too much.
Has your fear of balloons affected your relationships with family or friends?

I mean, my friends and family are mostly just... well, Mark is supportive, like I said. But honestly, I can't even really focus on that right now because my mind is just so completely stuck on what I was just telling you about work. I know you asked about my friends, but it's my job that's really taking the hit here, and that's what's keeping me up at night. 

I just... I can't get over the fact that it has actually started affecting my work. Like I was saying a minute ago, having to constantly hand off those normal classroom celebrations to my aides... it's just eating away at me. I'm the lead teacher, you know? I'm the one who should be in there creating those memories with the kids, and instead I'm making up excuses to stand in the hallway while Sarah and Jessica do it all. 

And that art table at the festival... I just can't stop replaying it in my head. I spent so much time planning it, mixing all those specific paint colors, getting everything perfectly ready for the kids to do this big beautiful mural, and then I just completely missed helping with it because I couldn't walk past those stupid helium balloons. And the absolute worst part, the part that really makes my stomach drop, is that my supervisor noticed. Mrs. Higgins definitely noticed I wasn't running the station I had planned. I'm just so terrified she's going to think I'm slacking off or that I'm not dedicated to my students, and I do, I care so much! I'm supposed to be a professional, and instead I'm jeopardizing my career and my reputation because I'm hiding from party decorations. It's just humiliating, it really is.
Are you avoiding any social activities or events outside of work because of your fear of balloons?

Well, yes, outside of work, too, but... honestly, it all kind of blends together because the feeling is exactly the same whether I'm at a family barbecue or in my classroom. It's that same intense need to just get away. Like I was saying about the birthdays and the fall festival... that's exactly what I do in my personal life, too. I just avoid it. 

Lately, I’ve been asking my aides, Sarah and Jessica, to handle the birthday circles completely. I mean, I used to just kind of stand near the door, but now I physically have to step out of the room if a parent brings in a balloon bouquet. And moving away from festival tables... like that art station I was telling you about... I just couldn't do it. I had to physically put distance between myself and those helium balloons tied to the ticket booth. 

And if I absolutely *have* to stay in a situation where there are balloons—like, say, if we're at a friend's house for a baby shower or something and I can't just leave without being incredibly rude, or if I'm at work and Mrs. Higgins is right there watching me—I just... I try to keep my distance as much as humanly possible. I'll stand in the farthest corner of the room, or I'll position myself behind a tall piece of furniture, and I just focus all my energy on getting through it without looking at them. I literally will stare at the floor, or stare at my shoes, or pretend I'm intensely interested in the pattern on my paper plate, just so I don't have to see them bobbing around. It takes every ounce of energy I have just to endure it until I can finally leave. It's exhausting, it really is. It just drains me completely.
Are there any everyday activities at home that you avoid or find difficult to do because of your fear of balloons?

No, no, not really at home. I mean, it's just Mark and me at the house, and obviously, he knows not to bring any balloons inside. So our home is... well, it's my safe zone, I guess you could say. It's the one place where I can just completely let my guard down and not have to scan the room the second I walk through the door. 

I don't have to worry about opening the front door and finding a surprise balloon bouquet sitting on the counter, or walking into the living room and seeing one of those foil balloons floating near the ceiling. It's just so peaceful knowing that when I cross that threshold, I don't have to be on high alert. I can actually just breathe. 

Because, honestly, that feeling of being on edge... it's just so draining. Like I was saying about having to stare at my shoes at parties or standing in the farthest corner of the room... it takes so much energy to constantly monitor where they are and how close they might get to me. But at home, I don't have to do any of that. I can just make dinner, or watch TV with Mark, or grade my students' papers—well, the ones I actually managed to collect without having to run out of the room because of a birthday party, anyway. 

So, yeah, home is fine. It's really just everywhere else that's the problem. It's the unpredictable places, the places where other people are in control of the environment, like my classroom or a friend's house or that fall festival... that's where I really struggle. But at home, no, I don't avoid anything because I know they won't be there.
Are you having trouble maintaining relationships with friends and family because of your fear of balloons?

I mean, I know you asked me about my friends and family earlier, and I know I kind of side-tracked onto work, but... well, no, not really. I wouldn't say I'm having trouble maintaining my relationships. I mean, my friends are still my friends, and my family is still my family. It's not like anyone has stopped talking to me because I don't want to be around balloons. 

It's more just... it's just the logistics of it all that gets complicated, you know? Like, if my sister is having a birthday party for my niece, I still want to go, I still love my niece, but I have to have this whole conversation with my sister beforehand about whether there are going to be balloons, and if there are, where are they going to be, and can she make sure they're tied down securely, and can she maybe put them in a room I don't have to go into... and I know it's exhausting for her to have to deal with my neuroses, and it's exhausting for me to have to ask, but she still invites me. She still loves me. 

And my friends, they're the same way. They know I have this... this issue. So if we're meeting up for dinner or something, they know not to pick a place that's likely to have some kind of big celebration going on with balloons everywhere. Or if someone is hosting a get-together at their house, they just know not to have them. So, no, the relationships themselves are fine. It's just... the things I have to do to *maintain* them, the hoops I have to jump through, the constant vigilance... that's the hard part. It's the mental load of it all, not the people themselves. They're all very understanding, for the most part. It's just me. It's just my own brain making everything so difficult.
Have you ever turned down a social invitation because you suspected there might be balloons present?

No, I don't think I've ever just flat-out said no to an invitation just because I thought there might be balloons. I mean, I can see why you'd ask that, because honestly, it would probably be a lot easier, wouldn't it? Just staying home where it's safe with Mark, where I know the environment is completely controlled. But no, I really try not to let it dictate my social calendar to that extreme. 

Like I was saying about my sister and my friends, I still want to be involved in their lives. I don't want to be the friend who just disappears and misses all the important milestones because of... well, because of this whole thing. So if I get an invitation to, say, a baby shower or a graduation party—which, let's be honest, are basically ground zero for helium balloons—I don't just check the 'will not attend' box on the RSVP. 

Instead, I go into this whole... like, reconnaissance mode. I'll text the host, or I'll call a mutual friend who's helping set up, and I'll just casually try to find out what the decoration situation is. I have to ask all those exhausting questions I mentioned earlier. And if there are going to be balloons, I just... I plan around it. I figure out exactly where they'll be, I plan where I'm going to sit, like I said before, finding that farthest corner or that tall piece of furniture to hide behind. 

It takes a massive amount of mental preparation. I'll probably be anxious the entire week leading up to the event, playing out all these scenarios in my head about where the balloon weights might be placed or if they're going to have those awful loose ones just rolling around on the floor... but I still go. I really do force myself to go because I don't want to miss out on celebrating the people I care about. So, turning down an invite completely? No, I haven't actually done that. I just make it incredibly, ridiculously complicated for myself to actually walk through the door.
Do you feel like your fear of balloons is significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy social events or perform your job as a kindergarten teacher?

Well, yes, honestly, it really is. I mean, social events are one thing, like I was just saying, I still go to them, but "enjoying" them? That's a stretch. I'm usually so focused on where the balloons are, monitoring every little breeze in the room to see if they're shifting, that I can barely focus on the conversation I'm having. I'll be nodding along to my friend talking about her new job, but in my head, I'm just calculating the distance between me and that foil 'Happy Birthday' monstrosity tied to the gift table. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm really enjoying those events. I'm just surviving them.

But work... work is where it's really starting to become a problem. A significant problem. Because as a kindergarten teacher, celebrations are just... they're baked into the curriculum, you know? It feels like every other week it's someone's birthday, or a holiday, or a hundred days of school, or whatever. And parents *love* to bring in balloons. I used to be able to just sort of manage it, maybe stand by the door, but lately, it's gotten to the point where I actually have to hand off the normal classroom celebrations to my teacher's aides. 

Like, little Timmy's mom will walk in with a dozen helium balloons, and I literally have to just... leave. I'll make up some excuse about needing to run to the office for copies, and I'll ask my aide, Sarah—who is an angel, bless her, but it's not her job to run the whole party—to take over. I just hide in the staff lounge until I know the balloons have been sent home. And it breaks my heart because I want to be there for my students, I want to sing 'Happy Birthday' and hand out the cupcakes, but I just can't be in that room.

And then there was the fall festival last month. I had spent weeks, literally weeks, planning this beautiful leaf-rubbing art table. I gathered all the supplies, I made these little example posters... I was so excited about it. But when I got there to set up, the PTA had decided to decorate the entire gymnasium with these massive balloon arches. Just everywhere. Archways over the doors, clusters on the bleachers. I tried, I really tried to just keep my head down and walk to my table, but my chest got so tight, and I started shaking, and I just... I had to leave. I missed the entire thing. I missed helping with the table I had planned. 

And the worst part is, my supervisor noticed. She asked me about it on Monday, why I wasn't at my station, and I had to mumble something about feeling under the weather, but I know she knows something is up. You can't just abandon your post at a major school event and not have people notice. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering. It's affecting my job, it's affecting how my supervisor sees me... it's just becoming this huge, unmanageable thing that's spilling over into every part of my life.
Do you feel like your fear of balloons is causing you significant emotional distress?

I mean... yes. God, yes. If you mean, like, am I just constantly upset about it? Then yes, absolutely. It's just so... it's so embarrassing, you know? I'm a thirty-year-old woman, I have a college degree, I'm responsible for a whole classroom of five-year-olds, and I am reduced to absolute tears over a piece of rubber filled with air or helium. 

The guilt is probably the heaviest part of it all. I go home after something like that fall festival, and I just cry. I sit on the couch with Mark and I just weep because I feel so entirely broken. Like, why can't I just be normal? Why can't I just go to a school event and help kids with their art projects without falling apart? 

And it's this horrible cycle, right? Because I get so worked up about the balloons, and then I feel guilty for being worked up, and then I just feel so down and pathetic because I feel like I'm burdening everyone around me. My sister, my teacher's aide Sarah, my husband... Mark is so patient, he really is, but I know it has to be exhausting for him to watch me spiral over something so mundane. I just feel this immense, heavy... I don't even know if 'distress' is a big enough word for it. It's just this constant, exhausting shadow over everything I do. I just feel so incredibly stupid and helpless all the time because of it, and I'm just so tired of living like this.
Do you believe your fear of balloons is something that you cannot control?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, if I could control it, I wouldn't be sitting here talking to you about it, right? It's the complete lack of control that makes it so maddening. Because logically—and this is the part that really gets to me, because the logical part of my brain is fully functioning and I know better—I know exactly what's happening. Like, I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just a decoration. It's just a piece of latex. Little Timmy's mom brought it in to be festive, it's meant to be fun, it's not an actual threat to my safety. 

I tell myself that, I really do. I'll literally stand there and have this whole internal monologue where I'm saying, "It's just a decoration, you are a grown woman, you are fine." But then... then I actually look at it. And if I see one, especially when they are blown up so much that the rubber is stretched incredibly tight, you know what I mean? Where it looks almost translucent and you just know it's at maximum capacity and about to give. 

And then when it's just bobbing there near the children... because kids are so unpredictable, right? They're always waving their arms around, they're jumping, they have sharp little pencils and scissors on their desks. I see that balloon just bobbing near them and my brain completely overrides all that logic I was just trying to use. It feels, in that exact second, like it could burst right in my face. Even if I'm standing all the way across the room by the chalkboard! It's this immediate, overwhelming reaction, and I get scared in a way that seems... well, just so much bigger than the situation. 

I mean, I know it's just a party favor, but my brain reacts like it's a live explosive that's about to go off. The fear is just completely out of proportion to what's actually happening in that room, and no matter how hard I try to rationalize it or talk myself down, I can't stop that terror from washing over me. So, no, I really don't feel like I have any control over it at all. It just completely takes over.
Do you think your fear of balloons is affecting your overall quality of life?

I know I kind of already dumped a lot of this on you a few minutes ago, but yes, absolutely. It really is. Because, like I was saying earlier, it has started heavily affecting my work, and my work is a huge part of my life. I went to college to be a teacher, I love my job, I love my kids, but now I’m in this position where I literally have to hand off normal classroom celebrations to my aides. 

And I know I mentioned Sarah taking over for me, but every time I have to do that, it just chips away at my confidence. It takes such a toll on you, you know? Waking up and wondering if today is the day someone brings in a birthday treat and I have to flee my own classroom. It just makes me feel like I’m failing at this career I worked so hard for. 

And then... well, I know I already brought up the fall festival, but that's just the perfect example of how much this is ruining things for me. I had planned that whole art table, I was so invested in it, I spent weeks getting the supplies ready, and I just completely missed helping with it because I couldn't handle being in the same gymnasium as those balloon arches. I just had to walk away from my own project. 

And the fact that my supervisor noticed I was gone... that just terrified me. It's one thing to struggle internally, or to have my husband or my sister know about it, but when your boss realizes you've abandoned your post at a major event... you start worrying about your job security, your reputation, what the parents are going to think. So when you ask about my overall quality of life, it's just... it's all intertwined. I can't be the teacher I want to be, I can't just enjoy a simple school event, and I'm constantly worried about who is noticing my absences. It just consumes absolutely everything.
Do you believe that your fear of balloons is excessive or unreasonable?

Yeah, I mean, I know I was literally just rambling about this exact same thing a minute ago, but yes. Absolutely. It is completely unreasonable, and I am so, so aware of how excessive it is. 

Like I was saying before, I know—intellectually, as a rational adult—that a balloon sitting in my classroom is probably just there as a decoration. It's supposed to be fun and festive for the kids. But the second I see one, especially if it's blown up so much that the rubber is stretched completely tight... you know, when it gets that shiny, almost see-through look where it's just stretched to its absolute breaking point? My brain just stops working. 

And when it's just bobbing right there near the children—because five-year-olds never sit still, they're always running past it or waving their hands or bumping into the tables—it literally feels like that thing could burst right in my face at any second. Even if I'm on the other side of the room! I get scared in a way that just seems so much bigger than the actual situation. I mean, it’s just a piece of latex and air! It shouldn't cause this level of sheer panic. 

So, yes, 'unreasonable' is exactly the word for it. It's completely out of proportion, and I think that's why I talk in circles about it so much, because it just baffles me. It's so frustrating to know exactly how excessive my reaction is, to be able to sit here and tell you how silly it is, and yet still feel that exact same overwhelming terror every single time I see one of those things just floating there.
How long have you been experiencing this intense fear of balloons?

Well, it hasn't been my whole life, if that's what you're wondering. It actually started pretty recently, all things considered. I'd say it's been about seven months now. And I know exactly when it started, too, because it was during this big children's art celebration we were having at the school. 

We had set up all these stations, you know, with finger painting and clay and those little tissue paper collages. The kids were having an absolute blast, and the parents were there, and of course, the PTA had brought in all these decorations. Including balloons. Lots of them. They were tied to the backs of the little chairs and bunched up by the doorways. 

I was kneeling down next to one of my students—I think it was Leo, he was working on this very intense macaroni necklace—and I was just leaning in to help him tie the string. There was a balloon tied to the chair right next to us. And I don't even know what happened, honestly. Maybe it brushed against a sharp edge of the table, or maybe it was just over-inflated, like I was talking about earlier. But it just... it popped. 

And it was right by my face. I mean, inches away from my ear. The sound was just deafening, like a gunshot going off right next to my head, and I actually felt the rush of air and the little pieces of latex hit my cheek. I screamed. I literally screamed in front of all my students and their parents, and I dropped the macaroni everywhere. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out right there in the middle of the art show. 

Ever since that exact moment, about seven months ago, I just haven't been the same. That's when this whole nightmare started. I can't even look at them now without flashing back to that exact second, that horrible loud crack and the feeling of it hitting my face. So, yeah, seven months of this completely taking over my life.
Do you believe that your fear of balloons is disrupting your daily life to the point where you feel it is a significant problem that needs to be addressed?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, one hundred percent. I mean, I know I've been talking your ear off about this, and I feel like a broken record, but it really has become this massive, unavoidable problem. It's not just a little quirk anymore, you know? It's completely disrupting my life, especially my work, which is just... it's devastating to me. 

Like I was saying earlier about having to hand off the classroom celebrations to my aides—that's a huge part of being a kindergarten teacher! You want to be the one handing out the cupcakes, singing the songs, seeing their little faces light up. And instead, I'm hiding in the hallway or the staff lounge because someone brought in a bouquet of balloons. I have to pull Sarah aside and say, "Hey, can you take over?" and I just feel so incredibly guilty and unprofessional every single time. 

And then, of course, there was that fall festival I mentioned. That was just... that was the breaking point for me, I think. I had spent weeks planning that art table. I had all the supplies organized, I was so excited to do the leaf rubbings and the pumpkin painting with the kids, and then I walk into the gymnasium and there are those massive balloon arches everywhere. And I just couldn't do it. I couldn't walk in. I had to completely abandon this project I had poured my heart into. 

And the worst part, the part that really made me realize this is a significant problem that I have to fix, was that my supervisor noticed. She noticed I wasn't at my station. When your boss sees you basically ditching a major school event, it's not just a personal struggle anymore; it's a professional liability. I can't have my supervisor thinking I'm unreliable or that I can't handle my job, all because of some balloons. So, yes, it's a massive disruption, and I desperately need to figure out how to get past it because I can't keep living like this, constantly on edge and missing out on my own life.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that the second I spot balloons at school, even across the hallway, my chest tightens and I freeze for a moment before I can think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing.

And the fact that my supervisor noticed I was gone... that just terrified me. It's one thing to struggle internally, or to have my husband or my sister know about it, but when your boss realizes you've abandoned your post at a major event... you start worrying about your job security, your reputation, what the parents are going to think. So when you ask about my overall quality of life, it's just... it's all intertwined. I can't be the teacher I want to be, I can't just enjoy a simple school event, and I'm constantly worried about who is noticing my absences. It just consumes absolutely everything.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's fear of balloons meets the criteria for a specific phobia
doctor.question: Do you believe that your fear of balloons is excessive or unreasonable?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, but when I see one stretched tight or bobbing near the children, it feels like it could burst right in my face and I get scared in a way that seems bigger than the situation.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the fear is excessive or unreasonable, which directly maps to the criterion that the fear is out of proportion to the actual danger.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, I know I was literally just rambling about this exact same thing a minute ago, but yes. Absolutely. It is completely unreasonable, and I am so, so aware of how excessive it is. 

Like I was saying before, I know—intellectually, as a rational adult—that a balloon sitting in my classroom is probably just there as a decoration. It's supposed to be fun and festive for the kids. But the second I see one, especially if it's blown up so much that the rubber is stretched completely tight... you know, when it gets that shiny, almost see-through look where it's just stretched to its absolute breaking point? My brain just stops working. 

And when it's just bobbing right there near the children—because five-year-olds never sit still, they're always running past it or waving their hands or bumping into the tables—it literally feels like that thing could burst right in my face at any second. Even if I'm on the other side of the room! I get scared in a way that just seems so much bigger than the actual situation. I mean, it’s just a piece of latex and air! It shouldn't cause this level of sheer panic. 

So, yes, 'unreasonable' is exactly the word for it. It's completely out of proportion, and I think that's why I talk in circles about it so much, because it just baffles me. It's so frustrating to know exactly how excessive my reaction is, to be able to sit here and tell you how silly it is, and yet still feel that exact same overwhelming terror every single time I see one of those things just floating there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of balloons is persistent and long-standing
doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing this intense fear of balloons?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about seven months, ever since a balloon burst close to my face during a children’s art celebration.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about how long I have been experiencing this intense fear, which corresponds to the duration of my symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, it hasn't been my whole life, if that's what you're wondering. It actually started pretty recently, all things considered. I'd say it's been about seven months now. And I know exactly when it started, too, because it was during this big children's art celebration we were having at the school. 

We had set up all these stations, you know, with finger painting and clay and those little tissue paper collages. The kids were having an absolute blast, and the parents were there, and of course, the PTA had brought in all these decorations. Including balloons. Lots of them. They were tied to the backs of the little chairs and bunched up by the doorways. 

I was kneeling down next to one of my students—I think it was Leo, he was working on this very intense macaroni necklace—and I was just leaning in to help him tie the string. There was a balloon tied to the chair right next to us. And I don't even know what happened, honestly. Maybe it brushed against a sharp edge of the table, or maybe it was just over-inflated, like I was talking about earlier. But it just... it popped. 

And it was right by my face. I mean, inches away from my ear. The sound was just deafening, like a gunshot going off right next to my head, and I actually felt the rush of air and the little pieces of latex hit my cheek. I screamed. I literally screamed in front of all my students and their parents, and I dropped the macaroni everywhere. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out right there in the middle of the art show. 

Ever since that exact moment, about seven months ago, I just haven't been the same. That's when this whole nightmare started. I can't even look at them now without flashing back to that exact second, that horrible loud crack and the feeling of it hitting my face. So, yeah, seven months of this completely taking over my life.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of balloons meets the criteria for a specific phobia
doctor.question: Do you believe that your fear of balloons is disrupting your daily life to the point where you feel it is a significant problem that needs to be addressed?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started affecting my work because I have to hand off normal classroom celebrations to aides and I missed helping with a festival art table I had planned, which my supervisor noticed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the fear is disrupting my daily life and causing a significant problem, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. Yes, one hundred percent. I mean, I know I've been talking your ear off about this, and I feel like a broken record, but it really has become this massive, unavoidable problem. It's not just a little quirk anymore, you know? It's completely disrupting my life, especially my work, which is just... it's devastating to me. 

Like I was saying earlier about having to hand off the classroom celebrations to my aides—that's a huge part of being a kindergarten teacher! You want to be the one handing out the cupcakes, singing the songs, seeing their little faces light up. And instead, I'm hiding in the hallway or the staff lounge because someone brought in a bouquet of balloons. I have to pull Sarah aside and say, "Hey, can you take over?" and I just feel so incredibly guilty and unprofessional every single time. 

And then, of course, there was that fall festival I mentioned. That was just... that was the breaking point for me, I think. I had spent weeks planning that art table. I had all the supplies organized, I was so excited to do the leaf rubbings and the pumpkin painting with the kids, and then I walk into the gymnasium and there are those massive balloon arches everywhere. And I just couldn't do it. I couldn't walk in. I had to completely abandon this project I had poured my heart into. 

And the worst part, the part that really made me realize this is a significant problem that I have to fix, was that my supervisor noticed. She noticed I wasn't at my station. When your boss sees you basically ditching a major school event, it's not just a personal struggle anymore; it's a professional liability. I can't have my supervisor thinking I'm unreliable or that I can't handle my job, all because of some balloons. So, yes, it's a massive disruption, and I desperately need to figure out how to get past it because I can't keep living like this, constantly on edge and missing out on my own life.
